323.title: Taking refuge formally
323.hook: many take the three refuges and five precepts before a monk or teacher
323.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists commonly repeat the three refuges and five precepts after a monk at temple gatherings; in Tibetan communities people take refuge from a lama and often receive a refuge name; in Zen a precepts ceremony (jukai) may include a dharma name and a small robe.

segments.voice: Yesterday: visiting a temple, and your line, shoes off. Did taking off your shoes at home feel, even for a second, like a small bow? Day three hundred twenty-three.

In a temple hall, a young woman kneels in front of an older monk. Her family sits behind her. The monk says a line in Pali, and she repeats it. He says the next, and she repeats that. Three lines, and then the same three again, and a third time. Then five short promises. It takes about three minutes. Nothing flashes, nobody cries, and afterward there's tea. But she will remember this morning for the rest of her life. Today: taking refuge formally.
screen: `A WOMAN KNEELS BEFORE A MONK.` → `THREE LINES, THREE TIMES.` → `FIVE SHORT PROMISES, THEN TEA.`

segments.voice: Here are the lines, in the Pali that Theravada Buddhists use: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge. I go to the teaching for refuge. I go to the community for refuge. Then again, with the word for second time, and again with the word for third time. Saying it three times marks it as meant. Then the five precepts, each one worded as a training rule: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life. From taking what isn't given. From sexual misconduct. From false speech. From intoxicants that cloud the mind. You met all of these, one by one, in the practices camp. Saraṇa means shelter: the place you run to in a storm. So refuge isn't joining a club or signing a creed. It's saying out loud where you turn when things get hard. Traditions do it differently. In the Theravada, people often repeat the refuges and precepts after a monk at many temple gatherings, again and again through life. In Tibetan communities there's a refuge ceremony with a lama, sometimes a tiny snip of hair, and a refuge name. In Zen, a ceremony of receiving the precepts may include a dharma name and a small sewn robe worn around the neck. What almost every teacher says is the same: there's no rush. Some people take refuge in their first month. Some never do, and practice for decades. The door stays open. When you're ready.
screen: `THREE LINES, SAID THREE TIMES.` · `FIVE TRAINING RULES.` · `SARANA — A SHELTER IN A STORM.` · `THERAVADA, TIBETAN, ZEN.` · then, large: `WHEN YOU'RE READY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice isn't a decision. It's a question to sit beside. Someday, would you want to take refuge formally? Maybe yes, maybe no, maybe you don't know. All three are fine answers. Just notice what comes up when you ask: curiosity, hesitation, warmth, nothing at all. Don't argue with it. Then let the question rest, and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Taking refuge formally. Saying the three refuges three times, and taking up the five precepts, before a monk or teacher, when you're ready.
Your line: when you're ready. Today, notice where you actually turn when something goes wrong. That's already an answer to what refuge means for you. Day three hundred twenty-three.

match.prompt: match the pieces of taking refuge.

myth: taking refuge is like signing a creed
it's saying where you turn when things are hard: the Buddha, the teaching, the community.
in the Theravada, people often repeat the refuges many times through life
at many temple gatherings, after a monk.
you have to take refuge within your first year of practice
teachers say there's no rush; some never do and practice for decades.

fork.setup: you've practiced for a year. a teacher mentions a refuge ceremony next month. you're honestly not sure. what do most teachers say?
options: decide now, or the chance is gone.
take your time; the door stays open.
only monks can take refuge.
fork.reveal: almost every teacher says there's no rush. some take refuge early, some never do, and the door stays open.

original.note: Pali saraṇa: shelter, refuge, as in Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, I go to the Buddha for refuge.

trapdoor: what you thought: taking refuge means converting.
what it means: saying aloud, three times, where you turn: the Buddha, the teaching, the community.
what a scholar hears: the threefold repetition (dutiyampi, tatiyampi) appears throughout the Pali canon, where lay followers declare refuge 'from this day forth, for life'.

324.title: The Buddhists you'll meet
324.hook: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, and many who simply sit: each a whole way
324.howItsDone: Buddhists practice through Theravada, Mahayana (including Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren) and Vajrayana traditions, and many lay Buddhists center their practice on giving, precepts, chanting and devotion rather than meditation; many others meditate in non-sectarian insight or mindfulness groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taking refuge formally, and your line, when you're ready. Did you notice where you turn when something goes wrong? Day three hundred twenty-four.

Picture a potluck at a big-city Buddhist center. A Vietnamese grandmother is quietly repeating the name of a Buddha under her breath. A Sri Lankan engineer mentions he'll be at the temple for the full moon. A young woman in a plain black robe has just come from a Zen sit. A Tibetan family arrives with a toddler and a thermos of butter tea. And a guy from the gym says he doesn't really call himself anything; he just sits every morning. They're all at the same table. Today: the Buddhists you'll meet.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER REPEATING A NAME.` → `A FULL MOON, A BLACK ROBE, BUTTER TEA.` → `A GUY WHO JUST SITS.`

segments.voice: Buddhists often speak of vehicles, yana, and you've now met all three. The Theravada, the way of the elders: Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, with the Pali canon, the alms round, the full-moon days. The Mahayana, the great vehicle, across China, Vietnam, Korea and Japan, with many schools inside it. Pure Land Buddhists recite the name of Amitabha Buddha, trusting in his vow; that's the grandmother at the potluck. Zen, called Chan in China and Seon in Korea, sits, and works with the koans you met a few weeks back. Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra. The Vajrayana, the diamond vehicle, in Tibet, the Himalayas and Mongolia, with mantra, the teacher and the day shaped by bodhicitta. And then there are many who simply sit: people in insight meditation groups, or with a meditation app, some of whom call themselves Buddhist and some of whom don't. Here's something that surprises newcomers. For many Buddhists in Asia, meditation isn't the center of practice at all. Giving, keeping the precepts, chanting, bowing, caring for the monastery and the family dead: that's the practice, and it's a whole one. Each of these is a complete way, with its own texts, teachers and saints. They disagree on real things, and they've learned from one another for centuries. This path has tried to show each one on its own terms, and never to rank them. So when you meet a Buddhist, don't assume. Ask what their practice looks like. You'll hear a different answer almost every time. Many doors.
screen: `THERAVADA — THE WAY OF THE ELDERS.` · `MAHAYANA — PURE LAND, ZEN, NICHIREN.` · `VAJRAYANA — THE DIAMOND VEHICLE.` · `MANY WHO SIMPLY SIT.` · then, large: `MANY DOORS.`

segments.voice: For this sit, picture that potluck table again. The grandmother, the engineer, the woman in the black robe, the Tibetan family, the guy from the gym. Let each one appear, and silently wish them well: may your practice go well. Then think of someone in your own life whose practice or faith differs from yours, and wish them the same. Rest in the breath, which all of them share. The bell holds the time.
The Buddhists you'll meet. Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, and many who simply sit: each a whole way, through its own door.
Your line: many doors. Today, greet someone whose practice differs from yours, and if the moment is right, ask them what it looks like. Then just listen. Day three hundred twenty-four.

match.prompt: match each Buddhist with a way.

myth: every Buddhist's practice centers on meditation
for many in Asia, giving, precepts, chanting and devotion are the heart of it.
Zen is called Chan in China and Seon in Korea
one school, several names across East Asia.
this path ranks the three vehicles from best to worst
each is shown on its own terms, as a whole way, never ranked.

fork.setup: at a gathering, you meet someone who says she's Buddhist. you've only learned about meditation. what's the best next move?
options: ask how long she meditates each day.
ask what her practice looks like.
tell her about your practice first.
fork.reveal: don't assume. her practice might be chanting, giving, devotion or sitting; almost every Buddhist gives a different answer.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali yāna: vehicle, as in Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna; Buddhist traditions describe their paths as vehicles.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism is one thing: meditation.
what it means: several whole ways, Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, and many who simply sit.
what a scholar hears: 'Hinayana', an old Mahayana polemical term, is avoided today; scholars and practitioners generally say Theravada for the living tradition of the elders.

sources.ref: Overview of living Buddhist traditions (Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana)
Larger Sukhavativyuha Sutra (Amitabha's vow, Pure Land)

325.title: Come and see
325.hook: many practice without taking refuge; the teaching invites you to come and see
325.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the Dhamma, including ehipassiko, in daily devotions; teachers across traditions welcome people to practice without taking refuge or calling themselves Buddhist.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Buddhists you'll meet, and your line, many doors. Did you get to ask someone what their practice looks like? Day three hundred twenty-five.

There's a certain kind of cook who, when you ask what's in the soup, doesn't explain. She just hands you a spoon. Don't take my word for it. Taste. It's a confident thing to do: it only works if the soup is good. This week has been about practicing with people, finding a sangha, a friend, a temple, maybe taking refuge someday. But plenty of people practice for years without any of that, and the teaching doesn't check anyone's ID at the door. It hands you a spoon. Today: come and see.
screen: `WHAT'S IN THE SOUP?` → `SHE HANDS YOU A SPOON.` → `TASTE IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Every day in Theravada temples, people chant a short list of the qualities of the Buddha's teaching. In Pali it begins: "Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko, akāliko, ehipassiko." In plain English: the teaching is well spoken by the Blessed One, visible here and now, not a matter of time, and ehipassiko. Ehi means come. Passa means see. Ehipassiko is a word made from an invitation: the teaching is the come-and-see kind. Not come and believe. Not come and sign. Come and see. The same list goes on to say it leads onward, and that the wise know it for themselves. You heard the same spirit with the Kalamas: test it yourself. And many of the old discourses end with a listener saying something like, it's as if you set upright what was overturned, or held up a lamp in the dark so those with eyes could see. The lamp shows. The seeing is yours. That's why so many people practice without any label. Some take refuge and some never do. Some come to the teaching through a temple and some through a library book or an app like this one. The invitation doesn't change. Now look back at a week of taking refuge in person. You need people. The whole of the path. Test it yourself. Shoes off. When you're ready. Many doors. And today, come and see. Tomorrow we begin the big lookout: six days to look back at the whole year, starting with the stories.
screen: `THE QUALITIES OF THE TEACHING.` · `EHI, COME. PASSA, SEE.` · `A LAMP HELD UP IN THE DARK.` · `NO LABEL NEEDED.` · then, large: `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, practice with no labels at all. You're not a Buddhist or a non-Buddhist for the next two minutes. You're just someone breathing, seeing what's here. Watch one breath all the way in and all the way out. Does watching it bring a little more ease, or not? Don't decide in advance. Come and see. The bell holds the time.
Ehipassiko. Come and see: the teaching invites you to look for yourself, not to believe first.
Your line: come and see. Today, practice one thing from this year without calling it anything, and watch what it does. Day three hundred twenty-five.

match.prompt: match the qualities of the teaching.

myth: ehipassiko means come and believe
it means come and see: the teaching is the kind you look at for yourself.
Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the teaching daily
the list begins 'svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo'.
you must take refuge before you're allowed to practice
many practice for years without any label; the invitation doesn't change.

fork.setup: a friend is curious about meditation but says, I'm not Buddhist and don't want to be. what does ehipassiko suggest you say?
options: then it isn't for you.
you don't need a label; try it and see what it does.
read ten books first.
fork.reveal: the teaching calls itself the come-and-see kind: it invites looking, not signing up.

original.note: Pali ehipassiko: from ehi (come) + passa (see): the come-and-see kind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slogan for skeptics.
what it means: one of the teaching's own qualities, chanted daily: it invites you to look for yourself.
what a scholar hears: ehipassiko turns the imperative 'ehi passa', 'come, see!', into an adjective; it stands in the Dhamma recollection (dhammānussati) between akāliko and opanayiko.

sources.ref: Dhammanussati (the recollection of the Dhamma), e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 11.12
Stock closing formula of the discourses ('as if one set upright what was overturned…')

326.title: Looking back: the stories
326.hook: the palace, the tree, the Deer Park, the sal trees
326.howItsDone: Buddhists retell the Buddha's life at festivals such as Vesak, in temple murals and in children's classes, and many keep images of the four great scenes: the birth, the awakening, the first teaching and the passing away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ehipassiko, and your line, come and see. Did you practice one thing without calling it anything, and watch what it did? Day three hundred twenty-six, and the big lookout begins.

At the end of a year, lots of people scroll back through their phone's photos. A birthday. A beach. A hospital waiting room. A dog. Things you'd forgotten, and things you never will. You're near the top of the first mountain now. For six days, we're going to turn around and look at the path behind you, one piece at a time. First, the stories: a whole life, from a palace to a grove of trees, that you've walked with since the start of the second camp. Today: looking back.
screen: `SCROLLING BACK THROUGH THE YEAR.` → `NEAR THE TOP OF THE FIRST MOUNTAIN.` → `FIRST, THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: The palace. A prince named Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, raised in three palaces, one for each season, with every comfort. Then four sights on the road with Channa: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a wanderer with a calm face. One night he looks back once at his sleeping wife Yasodhara and their newborn son, rides out on Kanthaka, and cuts off his hair by a river. The tree. Six years of starving himself, down to a handful of beans a day, until he remembers a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree as a boy. Sujata's bowl of rice. Eight handfuls of grass for a seat. I will not rise. Mara's army, and his hand reaching down to touch the earth. At dawn, awake. The Deer Park. Five old companions agree to ignore him, and then, as he comes near, they stand up. He teaches the middle way and the four truths, and Kondañña sees. The sal trees. Eighty years old, walking still, he eats his last meal from Cunda the smith, and lies down between two sal trees that bloom out of season. His last words, in Rhys Davids' old translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" And all around the four scenes, the people: Kisa Gotami and the mustard seed, the man with the finger garland who was told, I have stopped, you stop, and the Jataka animals, the hare in the moon and the golden goose. You don't need to remember every detail. What stays is the shape: comfort, a question, a long search, a seat under a tree, a teaching given away, a good death. The stories stay.
screen: `THE PALACE — FOUR SIGHTS.` · `THE TREE — I WILL NOT RISE.` · `THE DEER PARK — THEY STOOD UP.` · `THE SAL TREES — THE LAST WORDS.` · then, large: `THE STORIES STAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, choose one story from the year, whichever comes to mind first. Retell it to yourself from memory, silently, in a few sentences, as if to a child at bedtime. Don't check anything. Whatever you remember is what stayed. Then let the story settle, and sit with the breath, the way he sat under the tree. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The palace, the tree, the Deer Park and the sal trees: the whole life, from comfort to a good death, as it stays with you.
Your line: the stories stay. Today, tell one of this year's stories to someone else, a friend, a child, a partner, in your own words. Day three hundred twenty-six.

match.prompt: match each scene of the life.

myth: the five companions at the Deer Park refused to listen to him
they agreed to ignore him, then stood up to greet him as he came near.
the Buddha's last words urged diligence
in Rhys Davids' translation: work out your salvation with diligence.
the sal trees bloomed out of season at his passing
the story says they flowered as he lay between them.

fork.setup: you're the prince, starving yourself in the forest after six years. a memory comes back: a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree. what do you do?
options: push the memory away and fast harder.
accept a bowl of rice and try the quiet way.
go home to the palace.
fork.reveal: he took Sujata's rice, found a seat under the tree, and awoke by dawn: the middle way between comfort and starving.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit bodhi: awakening, the heart of the life story, and the name of the tree he sat under.

trapdoor: what you thought: a legend about a prince.
what it means: a life with a shape: comfort, a question, a search, awakening, teaching, a good death.
what a scholar hears: the full life appears only in later works such as the Nidanakatha and Buddhacarita; the early discourses tell it in scattered pieces (e.g. MN 26, MN 36, DN 16).

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta VI.10 (Digha Nikaya 16), the last words
Majjhima Nikaya 26 and 36 (the search and the awakening)
Nidanakatha (the four sights and the going forth)

327.title: Looking back: the practices
327.hook: metta, breath, walking, precepts, giving, the holy days
327.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists typically build a few practices into ordinary life: metta and breath meditation, walking meditation, keeping the five precepts, giving to monasteries and others, and keeping the moon days and festivals of their tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday: looking back at the stories, and your line, the stories stay. Did you tell one of them to someone in your own words? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Think about the first time you learned to cook something. You followed the recipe line by line, measured everything, checked the pan every thirty seconds. Years later you don't remember the lessons. You just cook. Your hands know when the onions are ready. Something like that has been happening all year. You've learned practices one at a time, often a little clumsily. Somewhere along the way, some of them stopped being lessons and started being things you do. Today: looking back at the practices.
screen: `FOLLOWING THE RECIPE LINE BY LINE.` → `YEARS LATER, YOU JUST COOK.` → `LESSONS BECOME WHAT YOU DO.`

segments.voice: Metta. Four phrases, wishing safety and ease, first to yourself, then to a benefactor, a dear friend, a neutral person, a difficult one, and finally to all beings, as the metta sutta puts it, like a mother protecting her only child. The breath. Sixteen steps of breathing mindfully: knowing the long breath and the short one, the whole body, joy and ease, the mind, and change. Counting when the mind is busy. Naming the hindrances when they arrive. Walking. A short lane, lifting, moving, placing, and the turn at the end, where you notice the wanting to turn before you turn. Walking in the city, too. The precepts. The three refuges and the five training rules, not killing, not taking, care in sex, true speech, a clear mind, and what to do when you break one: notice, make amends, begin again. Giving. Giving first, before you feel ready. The giver who is glad three times: before, while, and after. The poor woman's lamp that burned longest. Giving attention, and giving without a receipt. The holy days. The full and new moons of the uposatha, Vesak and the baby Buddha's bath, lanterns on the water, the rains retreat, and Kathina, when the robes are given. That's a lot. You won't keep all of it every day, and nobody does. The point was never to collect practices. It was to find the few that fit your life, and let them become what your hands already know. You practice now.
screen: `METTA — FROM YOURSELF TO ALL BEINGS.` · `THE BREATH AND THE LANE.` · `THE PRECEPTS AND GIVING.` · `THE HOLY DAYS.` · then, large: `YOU PRACTICE NOW.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, take a very quick tour. One metta phrase, silently, for yourself: may I be at ease. Three slow steps, lifting, moving, placing. One small precept, kept in mind for the next hour. One thing you could give today. Then sit, and let the breath be the whole practice, long or short, just as it is. Another day, try each one for a full minute. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Metta, the breath, walking, the precepts, giving and the holy days: the practices of the year, now yours to keep.
Your line: you practice now. Today, pick the one practice from this year that fits your life best, and do it once, on purpose. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

match.prompt: match each practice from the year.

myth: a good practitioner keeps every practice every day
nobody does; the point is to find the few that fit your life.
metta starts with wishing yourself well
then a benefactor, a dear friend, a neutral person, a difficult one, and all beings.
when you break a precept, the path says to give up
notice, make amends, and begin again.

fork.setup: you're giving something to someone. the Buddha says a giver can be glad three times. when?
options: before, while and after giving.
only when thanked.
when the gift is repaid.
fork.reveal: glad before giving, glad while giving, glad after: the gladness doesn't depend on thanks or return.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit bhāvanā: cultivation, bringing into being; the usual word for meditation and practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: practice means meditation.
what it means: a year of practices: metta, breath, walking, precepts, giving and the holy days.
what a scholar hears: the Pali canon groups merit-making into three bases, giving (dāna), virtue (sīla) and cultivation (bhāvanā), in AN 8.36, and the year's practices fall under all three.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37 (the giver glad three times)

328.title: Looking back: the Dhammapada
328.howItsDone: Buddhists across the Theravada world memorize and recite verses of the Dhammapada, hear them in sermons, and teach them to children; many keep a copy for a lifetime and return to favorite verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday: looking back at the practices, and your line, you practice now. Which one practice did you do on purpose? Day three hundred twenty-eight.

Most people have started a big book and never finished it. It sits on the nightstand with a bookmark stuck at page forty, quietly judging. This year you did something a lot of people never do. You read a whole book of scripture, cover to cover, a few verses at a time, over seventy-five days. At the end, you picked ten verses that stayed with you and wrote them down. Somewhere, maybe on a scrap of paper or in your phone, those ten are waiting. Today: looking back at the Dhammapada.
screen: `A BOOKMARK STUCK AT PAGE FORTY.` → `THIS YEAR, A WHOLE BOOK.` → `TEN VERSES, WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Dhammapada: the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching. Four hundred twenty-three verses in twenty-six chapters, the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings across the Theravada world, carried across Asia in several languages, and brought into English by Max Müller in the nineteenth century. You began with the twin verses. In Müller's translation, the very first line is: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." A few verses later came the one many people remember first: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Then the chapters rolled on. Earnestness. Thought, and the body fragile as a jar. Flowers. The fool and the wise. The thousands, where conquering yourself beats conquering a thousand thousand men. Evil and good, filling the water-pot drop by drop. Old age. Self. The Buddha, whose teaching fits in one line: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Happiness, where contentment is the greatest wealth. Anger. Other people's faults, so easy to see. The way. The elephant. Thirst, and the best gift, the gift of the teaching. And at the end, the mendicant and the brahmana, the one who is truly worthy. Here's something worth noticing. A verse you read months ago may mean something different now. That's not because the verse changed. You did. That's why people keep this book for a lifetime: not to finish it, but to come back. Twenty-six chapters, read whole. The verses stay.
screen: `423 VERSES, 26 CHAPTERS.` · `ALL THAT WE ARE — THE TWIN VERSES.` · `DROP BY DROP, CHAPTER BY CHAPTER.` · `SAME VERSE, DIFFERENT YOU.` · then, large: `THE VERSES STAY.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, find your ten verses, if you can: on paper, in your phone, wherever you wrote them. Read them slowly, once. If you can't find them, that's fine: let one verse you remember come to mind. Notice which verse lands differently now than it did when you first wrote it down. Then let the words go, and sit with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. The Dhammapada: four hundred twenty-three verses, twenty-six chapters, read whole, and ten of them yours.
Your line: the verses stay. Today, carry one of your ten verses with you, and let it meet one moment of your day. Day three hundred twenty-eight.

match.prompt: match the Dhammapada's chapters to what they taught.
pairs: drop by drop the pot fills

myth: the Dhammapada has 423 verses in 26 chapters
from the twin verses to the brahmana.
the first verse is about the body
in Müller's translation it begins: all that we are is the result of what we have thought.
a verse means exactly the same thing every time you read it
the verse doesn't change, but you do; that's why people come back.

fork.setup: you've read the whole Dhammapada. a friend asks: so you're done with it? what's the answer people who love the book usually give?
options: yes, finished.
no: you keep it for a lifetime and come back.
only monks need to read it twice.
fork.reveal: people keep this book for a lifetime, not to finish it but to come back: the same verse meets a different you.

original.note: Pali dhammapada: dhamma (the teaching) + pada (path, step, verse): the path of the teaching, or its verses.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book of nice quotes.
what it means: 423 verses in 26 chapters, the best-loved book of the Buddha's sayings, read whole.
what a scholar hears: besides the Pali, versions survive in Gandhari, in a Sanskrit Udanavarga and in Chinese, with overlapping but different verses.

329.title: Looking back: the depths
329.hook: the immeasurables, mindfulness, emptiness, koans, the elders, the diamond vehicle
329.tomorrow: The first mountain, from the top
329.howItsDone: Buddhists often spend years or a lifetime with one of these depths: the brahmaviharas, satipatthana practice, the Heart Sutra, koan study, or the Theravada and Tibetan paths, usually with a teacher and a community.

segments.voice: Yesterday: looking back at the Dhammapada, and your line, the verses stay. Did one of your ten verses meet a moment of your day? Day three hundred twenty-nine, the end of the week.

If you've ever snorkeled, you know the moment. From the boat, the sea is a flat blue surface. Then you put your face in the water, and there's a whole world down there: a reef, colors, a turtle drifting past as if it had all day. And you realize the flat blue was never the whole story. The last hundred days have been that moment. The stories, the practices and the book were the surface. The fifth camp put your face in the water. Today: looking back at the depths.
screen: `FROM THE BOAT, FLAT BLUE.` → `FACE IN THE WATER.` → `A WHOLE WORLD DOWN THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the four immeasurables, four rooms to live in: metta, karuna, mudita and upekkha. Loving-kindness, compassion, gladness at others' joy, and equanimity, each with a near enemy that looks like it, pity for compassion, indifference for equanimity. Then the Satipatthana, the direct path: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience, watched ardently, aware and mindful. The second arrow you don't have to shoot. Knowing without fixing. Seven years, or seven days. Then the Heart Sutra, the shortest great sutra. Form is emptiness, and emptiness is not nothing. No eye, no ear. Nothing to attain, and so, without fear. Gate, gate. Then the koans, which you weren't supposed to solve. Mu. Wash your bowl. The flag and the wind. Every day is a good day. The sound of one hand. Then two electives, side by side, never ranked. The way of the elders: three baskets, forest monks, rules as a shelter, calm and insight, rising and falling, entering the stream, Buddhaghosa's path of virtue, calm and wisdom. And the diamond vehicle: the six syllables, wheels and flags, the four thoughts, the teacher, tonglen, the slogans, bodhicitta, Tara, the sand swept into the river, the bardo. Each of these could fill a lifetime, and for many people, it does. You've had a first look. The Buddha said the teaching he found was deep and hard to see. Now you know a little of what he meant. Look back at the week, too: when you're ready. Many doors. Come and see. The stories stay. You practice now. The verses stay. And today: there's more.
